sense: by a promise, an oath or a kindness

terms.gloss: bind, oblige, put under an obligation
terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation: the person in the accusative, the bond in the ablative, the person bound to in the dative
evidence: Cic. Leg. 2.41: vōtī spōnsiō, quā obligāmur deō (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Bind by a vow, an oath, a contract or a kindness: obligātus eī nihil eram, “I owed him nothing” (Cic. Fam. 6.11.1, Lewis & Short). Literally “tie up, bandage” (rare); it also means “pledge, mortgage” and, with a crime, “make guilty of” (Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation: the person in the accusative, the bond in the ablative
evidence: Caes. BG 1.9: quam plūrimās cīvitātēs suō sibi beneficiō habēre obstrictās volēbat (Lewis & Short)
Caes. BG 1.31; Tac. A. 1.14, of binding by an oath (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The classical sense of the word (Lewis & Short): bind by an oath, a law, a kindness or a debt (aere aliēnō, Cic. Fam. 11.10.5). With sē and a crime it is “make oneself guilty of”; literally “tie up” (Plautus), rare.

phrases.latin: prīncipēs sint patria et parentēs, quōrum beneficiīs maximīs obligātī sumus
phrases.english: first should come our country and our parents, to whom we are bound by the greatest kindnesses

phrases.latin: gaudent mūneribus, sed nec data imputant nec acceptīs obligantur
phrases.english: they love gifts, but they neither count what they give nor feel bound by what they receive

phrases.latin: quam plūrimās cīvitātēs suō sibi beneficiō habēre obstrictās volēbat
phrases.english: he wanted to have as many states as possible bound to him by his own kindness
